patients.label: 51-year-old male kidney recipient with adaptive glomerular hypertrophy and subsequent FSGS

identity_evidence.quote: Patient 1 is a 51‐year‐old man with a BMI of 28.9 and a history of hypertension. The donor, a 52‐year‐old woman with drug overdose anoxia and a BMI of 22, had no other comorbidities. The posttransplant course was complicated by delayed graft function (DGF), posttransplant diabetes, and erythrocytosis. There was early CMV viremia and low‐level Class I donor‐specific antibody (DSA). Surveillance biopsies at 6 and 18 months were negative for rejection and showed progressive GH and development of FSGS in the second biopsy (Figures 1(A), 1(B), and 1(C)). Graft function continued to improve until the last follow‐up 36 months posttransplant (Scr: 1.41 mg/dL, eGFR: 59).

patients.label: 57-year-old female ADPKD kidney recipient with FSGS and progressive graft failure

identity_evidence.quote: Patient 2 is a 57‐year‐old woman with a history of ADPKD and hypertension, who received a kidney transplant 8 years earlier, from a deceased donor kidney from a 52‐year‐old with a kidney donor profile index of 71% and a BMI of 27.3. The posttransplant course was complicated by DGF, CMV viremia, and leucopenia. There was never rejection or the presence of DSA. The patient was obese at transplantation, with a BMI of 44.3. After transplantation, nutritional interventions resulted in progressive BMI reduction to 35.5 at the time of the last biopsy (Table 1). On a 12‐month surveillance biopsy, there was GH in comparison to the preimplantation and the 3‐week posttransplant biopsies. Graft function was stable (Scr: 1.2–1.3 mg/dL, eGFR: 41–55) until the 7th year posttransplant. A biopsy prompted by worsening creatinine and proteinuria on the 8^(th) year posttransplantation showed further increase in GH and the presence of FSGS (Figure 1(D)). Graft function continued deteriorating, and the patient was listed for retransplantation.

patients.label: 66-year-old kidney recipient at transplantation with late FSGS and death with functioning graft

identity_evidence.quote: Patient 3 was a 66‐year‐old with a history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus, when he received a deceased donor kidney from a 28‐year‐old male with an unknown history. The posttransplant course was complicated by DGF and resections of a native renal cell and colon carcinomas. The BMI was stable (23–26), and diabetes was well controlled (HBA1c: 7%–7.6%). The patient never experienced rejection or DSA and had stable graft function (Scr:1.2–1.4 mg/dL, eGFR: up to 65). The donor wedge biopsy, as well as an early posttransplant biopsy performed for DGF, demonstrated a good‐quality kidney with insignificant glomerulosclerosis and lack of fibrosis and vascular sclerosis. The glomeruli had a normal appearance and size. At the 17^(th) year, a biopsy for nephrotic range proteinuria showed prominent GH in comparison to the previous biopsies, as well as FSGS (Figure 1(E); Table 1). The patient died with a functioning graft, 13 months later, due to intestinal necrosis.
Patient 3 was a 66‐year‐old with a history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus, when he received a deceased donor kidney from a 28‐year‐old male with an unknown history.

To assess glomerular size, the largest diameter in nonsclerosed glomeruli was measured in 3 sections from each donor wedge (175–217 glomeruli) and 11 sections from each posttransplant biopsy (66–358 glomeruli) (Table 1). Glomeruli ≤ 140 µ were excluded in order to avoid the wide variation of incomplete/tangential glomerular cuts. claims.text: A 51-year-old man with hypertension received a kidney from a 52-year-old female donor with overdose anoxia and no other comorbidities. Posttransplant DGF, diabetes, erythrocytosis, early CMV viremia and low-level class I DSA were reported, without rejection. Serial 3/6/18-month biopsies documented glomerular size change and a perihilar FSGS lesion at 18 months, with initially normal and later focal abnormal EM. Initial sampling measurements and last IFTA cell have source caveats. At 36 months graft function continued to improve, serum creatinine 1.41 mg/dL and eGFR 59 with unreported prose eGFR units.

limitations: Three original recipient cases; deceased donors appear as explicitly other-subject characteristics and preimplantation graft specimens, not independent patient courses.
Actual-pixel analyses are in a separate visual submission. Figure 3 patient/specimen ownership is unresolved because caption and discussion do not identify which of the three cases supplied it.

Abstract says secondary FSGS/proteinuria developed at 3, 7 and >17 years, while detailed biopsies are 18 months, 8 years and 17 years. Abstract timing remains review-only. Patient 3 raw XML Table 1 last header prints 7y, conflicting with 17 years narrative/caption; table final measurements retain an unspecified time.
Printed eGFR units mil/min are retained literally in Patients 1/2 table, without automatic correction to mL/min or normalization to 1.73 m². Prose eGFR units are not stated.
Steroid tape and MP are retained as printed regimen names; no taper schedule, MP expansion, drug route/dose or absolute dates inferred.

IFTA Patient 1 last cell prints 0% (≈5%), an inconsistent score/percentage expression retained textually. Sampling variation footnote applies to Patient 1 first-biopsy diameter/proportion. Methods count ranges do not agree with every individual table count and are not used to overwrite those counts.
No source-listed supplements. No explicit same-patient prior-report identity links found; cited cohorts and theoretical therapies remain background.

Bare 0% glomerulosclerosis percentages do not negate FSGS: Patient 1 final 0% includes one focal lesion. Patient 2/3 bare 0% entries remain measurement facts without an invented focal-FSGS absence condition.

Patient 3 prose describes lack of fibrosis in donor wedge and early posttransplant biopsies, while Table 1 prints IFTA ≈5% and ≈10% for those samples. Both literal source representations retained; composite IFTA extent is not silently substituted for a pure fibrosis estimate, and no biological reconciliation is asserted.

Figure 1
Light microscopy images. (A) Representative image of 3‐month surveillance biopsy from Patient 1, with normal appearing glomeruli in a background of normal tubulointerstitium. caption_claims.text:
Figure 2
Electron microscopy images. (A) Six‐month surveillance biopsy from Patient 1 shows abnormally dilated capillary loops consistent with GH. The podocyte lining is normal with preserved foot processes of podocytes. (B) An eight‐year for‐cause biopsy from Patient 2 shows markedly dilated capillary loops in the patent glomeruli. The podocyte lining is abnormal with segments of effaced foot processes (arrow) and partially detached fragments of injured podocytes (arrowheads). FSGS was noted in one glomerulus (Figure 1(D)). (C) A seventeen‐year‐old biopsy from Patient 3 demonstrating patent capillary lumina (CL) in several loops. A podocyte body (PB) is noted on the bottom right, from which thin sheets of cytoplasmic fragments line an irregularly shaped pseudocystic space (arrows). Fragments of injured podocyte cytoplasm are noted between the arrowheads.

Patient 1 is a 51‐year‐old man with a BMI of 28.9 and a history of hypertension. The donor, a 52‐year‐old woman with drug overdose anoxia and a BMI of 22, had no other comorbidities. The posttransplant course was complicated by delayed graft function (DGF), posttransplant diabetes, and erythrocytosis. There was early CMV viremia and low‐level Class I donor‐specific antibody (DSA). Surveillance biopsies at 6 and 18 months were negative for rejection and showed progressive GH and development of FSGS in the second biopsy (Figures 1(A), 1(B), and 1(C)). Graft function continued to improve until the last follow‐up 36 months posttransplant (Scr: 1.41 mg/dL, eGFR: 59).

Glomeruli ≤ 140 µ were excluded in order to avoid the wide variation of incomplete/tangential glomerular cuts. Glomerular size can be assessed on light microscopy with available software [], but glomerular measurements are not routinely included in biopsy reports.

Patient 2 is a 57‐year‐old woman with a history of ADPKD and hypertension, who received a kidney transplant 8 years earlier, from a deceased donor kidney from a 52‐year‐old with a kidney donor profile index of 71% and a BMI of 27.3. The posttransplant course was complicated by DGF, CMV viremia, and leucopenia. There was never rejection or the presence of DSA. The patient was obese at transplantation, with a BMI of 44.3. After transplantation, nutritional interventions resulted in progressive BMI reduction to 35.5 at the time of the last biopsy (Table 1). On a 12‐month surveillance biopsy, there was GH in comparison to the preimplantation and the 3‐week posttransplant biopsies. Graft function was stable (Scr: 1.2–1.3 mg/dL, eGFR: 41–55) until the 7th year posttransplant. A biopsy prompted by worsening creatinine and proteinuria on the 8^(th) year posttransplantation showed further increase in GH and the presence of FSGS (Figure 1(D)). Graft function continued deteriorating, and the patient was listed for retransplantation.

claims.text: A 57-year-old woman with ADPKD/hypertension and obesity received a deceased 52-year-old donor kidney 8 years earlier. DGF, CMV viremia and leucopenia complicated the course; no rejection/DSA was reported. Nutritional interventions reduced BMI from 44.3 to 35.5. Graft function remained stable until year 7; serial 3-week/12-month/8-year biopsies showed increasing GH and eventual FSGS with worsening creatinine/proteinuria. The last table has creatinine 4.3 mg/dL, eGFR 12 printed mil/min and MACR 855 mcg/mgC. IF was negative in patent glomeruli with C3 specks in sclerotic glomeruli; EM showed approximately 50% patent-loop effacement. Continued graft failure led to retransplant listing, without a performed second transplant documented.

Patient 2 is a 57‐year‐old woman with a history of ADPKD and hypertension, who received a kidney transplant 8 years earlier, from a deceased donor kidney from a 52‐year‐old with a kidney donor profile index of 71% and a BMI of 27.3. The posttransplant course was complicated by DGF, CMV viremia, and leucopenia. There was never rejection or the presence of DSA. The patient was obese at transplantation, with a BMI of 44.3. After transplantation, nutritional interventions resulted in progressive BMI reduction to 35.5 at the time of the last biopsy (Table 1). On a 12‐month surveillance biopsy, there was GH in comparison to the preimplantation and the 3‐week posttransplant biopsies. Graft function was stable (Scr: 1.2–1.3 mg/dL, eGFR: 41–55) until the 7th year posttransplant. A biopsy prompted by worsening creatinine and proteinuria on the 8^(th) year posttransplantation showed further increase in GH and the presence of FSGS (Figure 1(D)). Graft function continued deteriorating, and the patient was listed for retransplantation.
All three patients received alemtuzumab induction with steroid tape

To assess glomerular size, the largest diameter in nonsclerosed glomeruli was measured in 3 sections from each donor wedge (175–217 glomeruli) and 11 sections from each posttransplant biopsy (66–358 glomeruli) (Table 1). Glomeruli ≤ 140 µ were excluded in order to avoid the wide variation of incomplete/tangential glomerular cuts. Mean glomerular diameters and percentage of glomeruli > 200 μm were compared using t and z tests, respectively.
Glomerular size can be assessed on light microscopy with available software [], but glomerular measurements are not routinely included in biopsy reports.

Patient 2: the IF sections contained 2 globally sclerosed and 2 normal appearing glomeruli. Immunostains were negative in the patent glomeruli, and specks of C3 positivity were noted in the sclerotic glomeruli.
Immunofluorescence (IF) studies for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, C1q, albumin, fibrinogen, and kappa and lambda light chains, with the following results.
(B) An eight‐year for‐cause biopsy from Patient 2 shows markedly dilated capillary loops in the patent glomeruli.
The podocyte lining is abnormal with segments of effaced foot processes (arrow) and partially detached fragments of injured podocytes (arrowheads).

(C–E) Images from the last biopsy of Patients 1, 2 and 3, demonstrating their respective focal segmental areas of glomerulosclerosis highlighted by arrows. There were no features of acute rejection. The remaining glomeruli were enlarged but otherwise normal on light microscopy.
The three patients presented in this report lacked inflammatory features, indicating allograft rejection, and overall showed only mild chronic features.

For Patient 2, obesity undoubtedly contributed to the burden of functional demands on the graft; despite some weight loss after transplantation, the BMI remained above 35.

limitations: Three original recipient cases; deceased donors appear as explicitly other-subject characteristics and preimplantation graft specimens, not independent patient courses.
Actual-pixel analyses are in a separate visual submission. Figure 3 patient/specimen ownership is unresolved because caption and discussion do not identify which of the three cases supplied it.

Abstract says secondary FSGS/proteinuria developed at 3, 7 and >17 years, while detailed biopsies are 18 months, 8 years and 17 years. Abstract timing remains review-only. Patient 3 raw XML Table 1 last header prints 7y, conflicting with 17 years narrative/caption; table final measurements retain an unspecified time.
Printed eGFR units mil/min are retained literally in Patients 1/2 table, without automatic correction to mL/min or normalization to 1.73 m². Prose eGFR units are not stated.
Steroid tape and MP are retained as printed regimen names; no taper schedule, MP expansion, drug route/dose or absolute dates inferred.

IFTA Patient 1 last cell prints 0% (≈5%), an inconsistent score/percentage expression retained textually. Sampling variation footnote applies to Patient 1 first-biopsy diameter/proportion. Methods count ranges do not agree with every individual table count and are not used to overwrite those counts.
No source-listed supplements. No explicit same-patient prior-report identity links found; cited cohorts and theoretical therapies remain background.

Bare 0% glomerulosclerosis percentages do not negate FSGS: Patient 1 final 0% includes one focal lesion. Patient 2/3 bare 0% entries remain measurement facts without an invented focal-FSGS absence condition.

Patient 3 prose describes lack of fibrosis in donor wedge and early posttransplant biopsies, while Table 1 prints IFTA ≈5% and ≈10% for those samples. Both literal source representations retained; composite IFTA extent is not silently substituted for a pure fibrosis estimate, and no biological reconciliation is asserted.

After transplantation, nutritional interventions resulted in progressive BMI reduction to 35.5 at the time of the last biopsy (Table 1). On a 12‐month surveillance biopsy, there was GH in comparison to the preimplantation and the 3‐week posttransplant biopsies. Graft function was stable (Scr: 1.2–1.3 mg/dL, eGFR: 41–55) until the 7th year posttransplant. A biopsy prompted by worsening creatinine and proteinuria on the 8^(th) year posttransplantation showed further increase in GH and the presence of FSGS (Figure 1(D)). Graft function continued deteriorating, and the patient was listed for retransplantation.

Patient 2 is a 57‐year‐old woman with a history of ADPKD and hypertension, who received a kidney transplant 8 years earlier, from a deceased donor kidney from a 52‐year‐old with a kidney donor profile index of 71% and a BMI of 27.3. The posttransplant course was complicated by DGF, CMV viremia, and leucopenia. There was never rejection or the presence of DSA. The patient was obese at transplantation, with a BMI of 44.3. After transplantation, nutritional interventions resulted in progressive BMI reduction to 35.5 at the time of the last biopsy (Table 1). On a 12‐month surveillance biopsy, there was GH in comparison to the preimplantation and the 3‐week posttransplant biopsies. Graft function was stable (Scr: 1.2–1.3 mg/dL, eGFR: 41–55) until the 7th year posttransplant. A biopsy prompted by worsening creatinine and proteinuria on the 8^(th) year posttransplantation showed further increase in GH and the presence of FSGS (Figure 1(D)). Graft function continued deteriorating, and the patient was listed for retransplantation.

Patient 2 is a 57‐year‐old woman with a history of ADPKD and hypertension, who received a kidney transplant 8 years earlier, from a deceased donor kidney from a 52‐year‐old with a kidney donor profile index of 71% and a BMI of 27.3. The posttransplant course was complicated by DGF, CMV viremia, and leucopenia. There was never rejection or the presence of DSA. The patient was obese at transplantation, with a BMI of 44.3. After transplantation, nutritional interventions resulted in progressive BMI reduction to 35.5 at the time of the last biopsy (Table 1). On a 12‐month surveillance biopsy, there was GH in comparison to the preimplantation and the 3‐week posttransplant biopsies. Graft function was stable (Scr: 1.2–1.3 mg/dL, eGFR: 41–55) until the 7th year posttransplant. A biopsy prompted by worsening creatinine and proteinuria on the 8^(th) year posttransplantation showed further increase in GH and the presence of FSGS (Figure 1(D)). Graft function continued deteriorating, and the patient was listed for retransplantation.

Figure 1
Light microscopy images. (A) Representative image of 3‐month surveillance biopsy from Patient 1, with normal appearing glomeruli in a background of normal tubulointerstitium. (B) Representative image of the 18‐month surveillance biopsy from Patient 1 showing significant GH in comparison to the previous biopsy. Occasional enlarged and irregularly shaped capillary loops are characteristic of GH (arrowheads). There is no evidence of acute rejection. Mild arteriolar hyalinosis and some tubular injury are noted. (C–E) Images from the last biopsy of Patients 1, 2 and 3, demonstrating their respective focal segmental areas of glomerulosclerosis highlighted by arrows. There were no features of acute rejection. The remaining glomeruli were enlarged but otherwise normal on light microscopy.

caption_claims.text:
Figure 2
Electron microscopy images. (A) Six‐month surveillance biopsy from Patient 1 shows abnormally dilated capillary loops consistent with GH. The podocyte lining is normal with preserved foot processes of podocytes. (B) An eight‐year for‐cause biopsy from Patient 2 shows markedly dilated capillary loops in the patent glomeruli. The podocyte lining is abnormal with segments of effaced foot processes (arrow) and partially detached fragments of injured podocytes (arrowheads). FSGS was noted in one glomerulus (Figure 1(D)). (C) A seventeen‐year‐old biopsy from Patient 3 demonstrating patent capillary lumina (CL) in several loops. A podocyte body (PB) is noted on the bottom right, from which thin sheets of cytoplasmic fragments line an irregularly shaped pseudocystic space (arrows). Fragments of injured podocyte cytoplasm are noted between the arrowheads.

Patient 2 is a 57‐year‐old woman with a history of ADPKD and hypertension, who received a kidney transplant 8 years earlier, from a deceased donor kidney from a 52‐year‐old with a kidney donor profile index of 71% and a BMI of 27.3. The posttransplant course was complicated by DGF, CMV viremia, and leucopenia. There was never rejection or the presence of DSA. The patient was obese at transplantation, with a BMI of 44.3. After transplantation, nutritional interventions resulted in progressive BMI reduction to 35.5 at the time of the last biopsy (Table 1). On a 12‐month surveillance biopsy, there was GH in comparison to the preimplantation and the 3‐week posttransplant biopsies. Graft function was stable (Scr: 1.2–1.3 mg/dL, eGFR: 41–55) until the 7th year posttransplant. A biopsy prompted by worsening creatinine and proteinuria on the 8^(th) year posttransplantation showed further increase in GH and the presence of FSGS (Figure 1(D)). Graft function continued deteriorating, and the patient was listed for retransplantation.

Patient 2 is a 57‐year‐old woman with a history of ADPKD and hypertension, who received a kidney transplant 8 years earlier, from a deceased donor kidney from a 52‐year‐old with a kidney donor profile index of 71% and a BMI of 27.3. The posttransplant course was complicated by DGF, CMV viremia, and leucopenia. There was never rejection or the presence of DSA. The patient was obese at transplantation, with a BMI of 44.3. After transplantation, nutritional interventions resulted in progressive BMI reduction to 35.5 at the time of the last biopsy (Table 1). On a 12‐month surveillance biopsy, there was GH in comparison to the preimplantation and the 3‐week posttransplant biopsies. Graft function was stable (Scr: 1.2–1.3 mg/dL, eGFR: 41–55) until the 7th year posttransplant. A biopsy prompted by worsening creatinine and proteinuria on the 8^(th) year posttransplantation showed further increase in GH and the presence of FSGS (Figure 1(D)). Graft function continued deteriorating, and the patient was listed for retransplantation.

patient_target.label: 66-year-old kidney recipient at transplantation with late FSGS and death with functioning graft

identity_evidence.quote: Patient 3 was a 66‐year‐old with a history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus, when he received a deceased donor kidney from a 28‐year‐old male with an unknown history. The posttransplant course was complicated by DGF and resections of a native renal cell and colon carcinomas. The BMI was stable (23–26), and diabetes was well controlled (HBA1c: 7%–7.6%). The patient never experienced rejection or DSA and had stable graft function (Scr:1.2–1.4 mg/dL, eGFR: up to 65). The donor wedge biopsy, as well as an early posttransplant biopsy performed for DGF, demonstrated a good‐quality kidney with insignificant glomerulosclerosis and lack of fibrosis and vascular sclerosis. The glomeruli had a normal appearance and size. At the 17^(th) year, a biopsy for nephrotic range proteinuria showed prominent GH in comparison to the previous biopsies, as well as FSGS (Figure 1(E); Table 1). The patient died with a functioning graft, 13 months later, due to intestinal necrosis.
Patient 3 was a 66‐year‐old with a history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus, when he received a deceased donor kidney from a 28‐year‐old male with an unknown history.

evidence.quote: (C–E) Images from the last biopsy of Patients 1, 2 and 3, demonstrating their respective focal segmental areas of glomerulosclerosis highlighted by arrows. There were no features of acute rejection. The remaining glomeruli were enlarged but otherwise normal on light microscopy.

Patient 3 was a 66‐year‐old with a history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus, when he received a deceased donor kidney from a 28‐year‐old male with an unknown history. The posttransplant course was complicated by DGF and resections of a native renal cell and colon carcinomas. The BMI was stable (23–26), and diabetes was well controlled (HBA1c: 7%–7.6%). The patient never experienced rejection or DSA and had stable graft function (Scr:1.2–1.4 mg/dL, eGFR: up to 65). The donor wedge biopsy, as well as an early posttransplant biopsy performed for DGF, demonstrated a good‐quality kidney with insignificant glomerulosclerosis and lack of fibrosis and vascular sclerosis. The glomeruli had a normal appearance and size. At the 17^(th) year, a biopsy for nephrotic range proteinuria showed prominent GH in comparison to the previous biopsies, as well as FSGS (Figure 1(E); Table 1). The patient died with a functioning graft, 13 months later, due to intestinal necrosis.

claims.text: A recipient age 66 at transplantation, with hypertension and diabetes, received a deceased 28-year-old male donor kidney of unknown history. Posttransplant DGF and resection of native renal-cell and colon carcinomas were documented. Earlier graft function/BMI were stable and diabetes well controlled. Donor and 2-week biopsies were described as good quality/normal glomerular size. A narrative 17th-year biopsy for nephrotic-range proteinuria showed GH/FSGS, but its table header prints 7y; final table values remain untimed: creatinine 1.41 mg/dL, eGFR 45 mL/min, MACR 4356 mcg/mgC, approximately 15% patent-loop effacement. IF weakly marked the segmental lesion with C3/IgM and highlighted tubular C3 droplets. Thirteen months after the narrative late biopsy he died from intestinal necrosis with a functioning graft.

Actual-pixel analyses are in a separate visual submission. Figure 3 patient/specimen ownership is unresolved because caption and discussion do not identify which of the three cases supplied it.

Abstract says secondary FSGS/proteinuria developed at 3, 7 and >17 years, while detailed biopsies are 18 months, 8 years and 17 years. Abstract timing remains review-only. Patient 3 raw XML Table 1 last header prints 7y, conflicting with 17 years narrative/caption; table final measurements retain an unspecified time.
Printed eGFR units mil/min are retained literally in Patients 1/2 table, without automatic correction to mL/min or normalization to 1.73 m². Prose eGFR units are not stated.
Steroid tape and MP are retained as printed regimen names; no taper schedule, MP expansion, drug route/dose or absolute dates inferred.

IFTA Patient 1 last cell prints 0% (≈5%), an inconsistent score/percentage expression retained textually. Sampling variation footnote applies to Patient 1 first-biopsy diameter/proportion. Methods count ranges do not agree with every individual table count and are not used to overwrite those counts.
No source-listed supplements. No explicit same-patient prior-report identity links found; cited cohorts and theoretical therapies remain background.

Bare 0% glomerulosclerosis percentages do not negate FSGS: Patient 1 final 0% includes one focal lesion. Patient 2/3 bare 0% entries remain measurement facts without an invented focal-FSGS absence condition.

Patient 3 prose describes lack of fibrosis in donor wedge and early posttransplant biopsies, while Table 1 prints IFTA ≈5% and ≈10% for those samples. Both literal source representations retained; composite IFTA extent is not silently substituted for a pure fibrosis estimate, and no biological reconciliation is asserted.

The patient never experienced rejection or DSA and had stable graft function (Scr:1.2–1.4 mg/dL, eGFR: up to 65). The donor wedge biopsy, as well as an early posttransplant biopsy performed for DGF, demonstrated a good‐quality kidney with insignificant glomerulosclerosis and lack of fibrosis and vascular sclerosis. The glomeruli had a normal appearance and size. At the 17^(th) year, a biopsy for nephrotic range proteinuria showed prominent GH in comparison to the previous biopsies, as well as FSGS (Figure 1(E); Table 1). The patient died with a functioning graft, 13 months later, due to intestinal necrosis.
At the 17^(th) year, a biopsy for nephrotic range proteinuria showed prominent GH in comparison to the previous biopsies, as well as FSGS (Figure 1(E); Table 1).
(C) A seventeen‐year‐old biopsy from Patient 3 demonstrating patent capillary lumina (CL) in several loops.
A podocyte body (PB) is noted on the bottom right, from which thin sheets of cytoplasmic fragments line an irregularly shaped pseudocystic space (arrows).
Fragments of injured podocyte cytoplasm are noted between the arrowheads.

(C–E) Images from the last biopsy of Patients 1, 2 and 3, demonstrating their respective focal segmental areas of glomerulosclerosis highlighted by arrows. There were no features of acute rejection. The remaining glomeruli were enlarged but otherwise normal on light microscopy.
Glomerular size can be assessed on light microscopy with available software [], but glomerular measurements are not routinely included in biopsy reports.

Patient 3 was a 66‐year‐old with a history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus, when he received a deceased donor kidney from a 28‐year‐old male with an unknown history. The posttransplant course was complicated by DGF and resections of a native renal cell and colon carcinomas. The BMI was stable (23–26), and diabetes was well controlled (HBA1c: 7%–7.6%). The patient never experienced rejection or DSA and had stable graft function (Scr:1.2–1.4 mg/dL, eGFR: up to 65). The donor wedge biopsy, as well as an early posttransplant biopsy performed for DGF, demonstrated a good‐quality kidney with insignificant glomerulosclerosis and lack of fibrosis and vascular sclerosis. The glomeruli had a normal appearance and size. At the 17^(th) year, a biopsy for nephrotic range proteinuria showed prominent GH in comparison to the previous biopsies, as well as FSGS (Figure 1(E); Table 1). The patient died with a functioning graft, 13 months later, due to intestinal necrosis.

Mean glomerular diameters and percentage of glomeruli > 200 μm were compared using t and z tests, respectively.
Glomerular size can be assessed on light microscopy with available software [], but glomerular measurements are not routinely included in biopsy reports.

Patient 3 was a 66‐year‐old with a history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus, when he received a deceased donor kidney from a 28‐year‐old male with an unknown history. The posttransplant course was complicated by DGF and resections of a native renal cell and colon carcinomas. The BMI was stable (23–26), and diabetes was well controlled (HBA1c: 7%–7.6%). The patient never experienced rejection or DSA and had stable graft function (Scr:1.2–1.4 mg/dL, eGFR: up to 65). The donor wedge biopsy, as well as an early posttransplant biopsy performed for DGF, demonstrated a good‐quality kidney with insignificant glomerulosclerosis and lack of fibrosis and vascular sclerosis. The glomeruli had a normal appearance and size. At the 17^(th) year, a biopsy for nephrotic range proteinuria showed prominent GH in comparison to the previous biopsies, as well as FSGS (Figure 1(E); Table 1). The patient died with a functioning graft, 13 months later, due to intestinal necrosis.
Glomerular size can be assessed on light microscopy with available software [], but glomerular measurements are not routinely included in biopsy reports.
